chapter_theme: The one song at Thiruvenjamakkoodal (திருவெஞ்சமாக்கூடல்): a short plea in three similes, the bee, the monkey and the ball, for grace that ends the mind; the Lord is seen by his servants and hidden from the stubborn.

931.reading: A short song: the poet asks to seek grace like a bee seeking nectar, to strike down the disease of time like a monkey, to play with the bond like a ball, and, his mind ended, to be taught and given grace. The praise names Murugan the one his servants see, the lord of the high vel dwelling in the forest shrine, not to be found by the stubborn, at Venjamakkoodal.
931.nuance: சிந்தை மாய்த்து: the mind is to be ended, not calmed. The three similes are compact and their sense is uncertain: the bee is clear, but what the monkey and the ball stand for (காலப் பிணி சாடி, பாசத்துடன் ஆடி) is my guess. தொண்டரால் காணப் பெறுவோனே against மிண்டரால் காணக் கிடையானே: devotion sees what stubborn pride cannot.

links.note: The song calls Murugan the one seen by his servants and not to be found by the stubborn (தொண்டரால் காணப் பெறுவோனே, மிண்டரால் காணக் கிடையானே). Tirumanthiram 1804 says the Lord entered the heart of his servant by grace and is not seen, though within, by those without grace (அகம்புகுந்தும் தெரியான் அருள் இல்லோர்க்கு). Both make seeing the Lord depend on the servant's state, not on his nearness.

source_issues: Song 931: unflagged garble மந்திபோற்ள (line 2), probably மந்திபோற்; ஏசித் (line 4) may be a corrupt தேசித் (teach).
